questions.q: Rutherford's alpha-scattering experiment established the existence of the:
questions.solution:
A very small fraction of alpha particles were scattered through large angles, and a few came almost straight back — which Rutherford called as surprising as a shell bouncing off tissue paper.

That required a **small, dense, positively charged nucleus** containing almost all the atom's mass, with the atom otherwise mostly empty space.

The nucleus is about $10^{-15}\ \text{m}$ across against the atom's $10^{-10}\ \text{m}$ — a factor of $10^{5}$, which is why most alphas passed through undeflected.

questions.q: In the Bohr model, the angular momentum of an electron in the $n$th orbit is:
questions.solution:
Bohr's quantisation condition is $mvr = \mathbf{\dfrac{nh}{2\pi}} = n\hbar$.

Bohr simply **postulated** it with no justification. De Broglie later supplied one: treating the orbit as a standing electron wave requires a whole number of wavelengths round the circumference,

$2\pi r = n\lambda = \dfrac{nh}{mv}$

which rearranges to exactly Bohr's condition. That is a genuinely satisfying moment — an arbitrary postulate turning out to be a standing-wave condition.

questions.q: Energy is released in both nuclear fission and fusion because in each case the products have:
questions.solution:
The binding energy per nucleon curve peaks near $A \approx 56$ (iron and nickel) at about $8.8\ \text{MeV}$.

**Fission** of a heavy nucleus and **fusion** of light ones both move the products **towards** that peak, so the binding energy per nucleon **increases** and the difference is released.

This is why iron is the end of the line for stellar fusion: past it, fusion would **consume** energy rather than release it, which is what triggers a supernova.

questions.q: In beta-minus decay, the atomic number of the nucleus:
questions.solution:
In $\beta^{-}$ decay a neutron converts into a proton, an electron and an antineutrino:

$n \rightarrow p + e^{-} + \bar{\nu}$

So $Z$ **increases by 1** while the mass number $A$ is **unchanged**.

Compare: **alpha** decay reduces $Z$ by 2 and $A$ by 4; **gamma** emission changes neither, being only a loss of excitation energy.

questions.q: The half-life of a radioactive sample is independent of:
questions.solution:
Radioactive decay is a **nuclear** process, and the nucleus is shielded from the chemical environment by the surrounding electrons.

So the half-life is **unaffected by temperature, pressure or chemical combination** — uranium in an ore decays at the same rate as uranium metal.

It is entirely fixed by the nuclide, through $t_{1/2} = \dfrac{0.693}{\lambda}$. That reliability is precisely what makes radiometric dating possible.

questions.q: The series of hydrogen spectral lines that falls in the visible region is the:
questions.solution:
The **Balmer** series, with transitions ending at $n = 2$, falls in the **visible** region.

The **Lyman** series ($n = 1$) is in the ultraviolet, since those transitions involve the largest energy gaps; the **Paschen** ($n = 3$) and beyond are in the infrared.

It is no accident that the Balmer series was discovered first — it is the one the eye can see.

questions.q: In a nuclear reactor, the moderator is used to:
questions.solution:
A **moderator** — graphite or heavy water — **slows fast neutrons** to thermal energies, because $\text{U}^{235}$ fissions far more readily with slow neutrons.

Light nuclei are used because a neutron loses most energy in a collision with a particle of similar mass, just as in an elastic collision between equal masses.

The **control rods**, of cadmium or boron, are the ones that **absorb** neutrons, and they regulate the chain reaction. The **coolant** carries away the heat. Three different jobs, three different materials.

questions.q: The mass of a nucleus is always less than the sum of the masses of its constituent nucleons. This difference is called the:
questions.solution:
The **mass defect** $\Delta m$ is that difference, and it is converted into the **binding energy** by

$E_b = \Delta m\,c^{2}$

The mass is missing because it was released as energy when the nucleons came together; supplying that same energy back is what it takes to pull them apart.

So mass defect and binding energy are the same fact in two units — which is as direct a demonstration of $E = mc^{2}$ as physics offers.

questions.q: The density of nuclear matter is:
options: Nearly the same for all nuclei
questions.solution:
Since $R = R_0A^{1/3}$, the volume $\propto R^{3} \propto A$, while the mass also $\propto A$.

So the density is **independent of $A$** and is nearly the same for every nucleus — about $2.3\times10^{17}\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$.

That is around $10^{14}$ times the density of water; a teaspoon of it would weigh a hundred million tonnes. It also implies nuclear matter is **incompressible**, and is essentially the density of a neutron star.

questions.q: Find the energy, in electronvolts, of the $n = 2$ level of hydrogen. Give the magnitude.
A radioactive sample has a half-life of $4$ days. What fraction remains after $12$ days? Give the answer as a decimal.
A nuclide has a decay constant of $0.0231\ \mathrm{day^{-1}}$. Find its half-life, in days.
A mass defect of $0.1\ \text{u}$ corresponds to how much energy, in MeV? Take $1\ \text{u} = 931\ \text{MeV}/c^{2}$.
questions.solution:
$E = \Delta m\,c^{2} = 0.1 \times 931 = \mathbf{93.1\ \text{MeV}}$.

The conversion $1\ \text{u} = 931\ \text{MeV}$ is worth memorising — it turns every mass-defect calculation into a single multiplication.

questions.q: Using $R = R_0A^{1/3}$ with $R_0 = 1.2\ \text{fm}$, find the radius of a nucleus with $A = 64$, in femtometres.

State Bohr's postulates and derive the expression for the energy of the $n$th orbit of the hydrogen atom. Explain how the model accounts for the hydrogen spectral series, and state two of its limitations.
questions.solution:
**The postulates.**

**1. Stationary orbits.** The electron revolves in certain permitted circular orbits **without radiating energy**, contrary to classical electrodynamics — which is asserted precisely because atoms manifestly do not collapse. A classical accelerating electron would spiral into the nucleus in about $10^{-8}\ \text{s}$.

**2. Quantisation of angular momentum.** Only those orbits are allowed for which

$mvr = \dfrac{nh}{2\pi}$, $n = 1, 2, 3 \ldots$

**3. Emission and absorption.** Radiation is emitted or absorbed only when the electron **jumps** between orbits, with

$h\nu = E_2 - E_1$

**Deriving the energy.**

The electrostatic attraction provides the centripetal force:

$\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{e^{2}}{r^{2}} = \dfrac{mv^{2}}{r}$

$mv^{2} = \dfrac{e^{2}}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r}$ ... (1)

**Kinetic energy** is therefore

$K = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^{2} = \dfrac{e^{2}}{8\pi\varepsilon_0 r}$

**Potential energy** of the electron in the nucleus's field:

$U = -\dfrac{e^{2}}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r}$

**Total energy:**

$E = K + U = \dfrac{e^{2}}{8\pi\varepsilon_0 r} - \dfrac{e^{2}}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r} = -\dfrac{e^{2}}{8\pi\varepsilon_0 r}$

Note $E = -K$, and the total energy is **negative**, meaning the electron is bound.

Now bring in quantisation. From postulate 2, $v = \dfrac{nh}{2\pi mr}$; substituting into (1) and solving gives

$r_n = \dfrac{n^{2}h^{2}\varepsilon_0}{\pi me^{2}}$, so $r_n \propto n^{2}$

Putting this into the expression for $E$:

$\boxed{E_n = -\dfrac{me^{4}}{8\varepsilon_0^{2}h^{2}n^{2}} = -\dfrac{13.6}{n^{2}}\ \text{eV}}$

**Accounting for the spectral series.** A jump from level $n_2$ down to $n_1$ emits a photon of energy

$h\nu = E_{n_2} - E_{n_1} = 13.6\left(\dfrac{1}{n_1^{2}} - \dfrac{1}{n_2^{2}}\right)\ \text{eV}$

which gives the Rydberg formula

$\dfrac{1}{\lambda} = R\left(\dfrac{1}{n_1^{2}} - \dfrac{1}{n_2^{2}}\right)$

Each series is defined by where the electron **lands**:

**Lyman**, $n_1 = 1$ — ultraviolet, the largest energy gaps

**Balmer**, $n_1 = 2$ — visible, and so the first to be discovered

**Paschen**, $n_1 = 3$ — infrared

**Brackett**, $n_1 = 4$, and **Pfund**, $n_1 = 5$ — far infrared

The triumph is that the Rydberg constant, previously an **empirical** number fitted to spectra, now emerges from $m$, $e$, $h$ and $\varepsilon_0$ — and the computed value agrees with the measured one. A formula that had merely described the lines was now derived from a model.

**Two limitations.**

**1. It fails for every atom with more than one electron.** The derivation assumes a single electron feeling only the nucleus. Add a second and the electron-electron repulsion makes the problem intractable this way; the model gets helium's spectrum badly wrong. It works for hydrogen and for hydrogen-like ions ($\text{He}^{+}$, $\text{Li}^{2+}$) and nowhere else.

**2. It contradicts the uncertainty principle.** A Bohr orbit specifies the electron's position **and** momentum simultaneously and exactly, which $\Delta x\,\Delta p \ge \dfrac{h}{4\pi}$ forbids. The orbit is not merely unmeasurable — it is not a meaningful description of where the electron is. This is why quantum mechanics replaced the **orbit** with the **orbital**, a probability distribution.

Other failures worth knowing: it cannot explain the **fine structure** of spectral lines seen at high resolution, the **Zeeman** and **Stark** splittings in magnetic and electric fields, or the **relative intensities** of the lines — it says which lines appear but not how bright they are.
